archetype.name: Dual-Threat (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 33-year-old career spot starter whose legs have been a top-tier part of his game for a decade, now working as Washington's QB2, winning underneath and on designed runs rather than pushing the ball downfield.

report.headline: Efficient insurance policy: short-game sharp, but his best numbers came when trailing big
report.take:
Marcus Mariota is Jayden Daniels' backup, listed QB2 as of November 17. Every number here comes from three scattered appearances. He played 45% of the snaps in relief at Dallas, every snap in the Week 3 win over Seattle, and only 16% of a Week 4 start against Indianapolis that ended early. Read the line as a backup's sample: 51 attempts, not a season. In that sample he has been good. A 0.173 EPA per dropback ranks 9th of 54 qualifiers. His +3.89 CPOE ranks 10th. He has no interceptions and no lost fumbles.

The engine is the short game. On throws under 10 air yards he completed 76.7% at 0.3 EPA per attempt, with CPOE of +8.9. Most of his value came from getting the ball out on schedule to Terry McLaurin, who produced 0.357 EPA per target on 13 looks. His aggressiveness dropped almost five points from last year, to 14.89%. That reads like a backup told to stay on script, not a different player. His career aDOT has swung between 7.5 and 10.2 depending on the offense. The legs remain real: two designed runs averaged 22 yards. He has ranked in the top dozen or so QBs in rushing yards in most seasons he played meaningful snaps.

The numbers hide two things. First, game state flatters him. When trailing by 9 or more he posted 0.495 EPA per play on 12 plays, much of it in the Dallas blowout against what is now the league's worst defense. In one-score situations, 42 plays, he was dead average at -0.006. Third down was poor: -0.263 EPA and a 26.7% conversion rate. Second, protection. He was pressured on 38.9% of dropbacks, worst among 42 charted QBs, yet sacked on only 14.3% of those pressures, 2nd best. His career says that won't hold. Pressure-to-sack rates of 36.5%, 41.7%, 37.8% and 31.4% in past seasons say he has always taken sacks when he extends plays.

Where it's heading depends entirely on Daniels. Nothing in this dossier suggests Daniels is unavailable for Week 11, so Mariota projects as a non-factor unless something changes. If he is pressed into starts, expect his 2025 shape. That means roughly league-average efficiency, solid rushing, a handful of picks the current zero is hiding, and more sacks behind a line missing Laremy Tunsil and guard Lucas Patrick.

strengths.title: Clean, accurate short passing
strengths.body: Under 10 air yards he has been precise and on time, the backbone of his positive EPA. That fits a veteran running a defined script with McLaurin as the main read. Accuracy has been a career-long trait: his CPOE ranked 13th in both 2018 and 2025. Expect it to hold in kind, if not quite at this rate.

strengths.title: Legs as a real weapon
strengths.body: Two designed runs went for 22 yards a carry with positive EPA, and he ran for 35 yards in his brief Week 4 start. He has been a top-10 rushing QB in yardage in several seasons, including 6th in 2022. At 33 the volume is down, but the run threat still forces defenses to account for him.

strengths.title: Zero turnovers so far
strengths.body: No interceptions and no turnover-worthy fumbles across 57 dropbacks, ranking 1st in INT rate. Some of that is the conservative, short-heavy approach. He threw 7 picks in 9 games last year, so treat the zero as a small sample, not a new skill.

concerns.title: Production skewed to trailing game script
concerns.body: His efficiency sits heavily in plays where Washington trailed by 9 or more. In one-score situations he was average. Defenses sitting on leads concede the short stuff he lives on. In a competitive start, expect his EPA to land much closer to league average.

concerns.title: Sack avoidance won't survive the pressure
concerns.body: He faced the heaviest pressure rate among charted QBs yet rarely went down. His history says the opposite: he has typically been near the bottom in turning pressure into sacks. With Tunsil on IR and Patrick out, the protection problem is structural. More sacks are likely in any extended action.

concerns.title: Third downs and the deep ball
concerns.body: On third down (7.4 yards to go on average) he converted only 26.7%. Downfield he completed 25% of eight throws, though two went for touchdowns. The TDs propped up his 7.8% TD rate, which will regress. Both samples are tiny, but they match a QB who wins on schedule rather than off it.

trend.note: Three appearances in three different roles: a relief stint in a blowout at Dallas, a full game in a win over Seattle, and a 16%-snap start against Indianapolis. He hasn't logged a pass since Week 4, so there is no trajectory, just a role that depends on Daniels.

nextGame.headline: Likely clipboard duty; if called on, Cincinnati's soft underneath defense suits him
nextGame.body:
Mariota is QB2, and nothing in the dossier flags Daniels as unavailable, so the base case is that he doesn't throw a pass. If he does play, Cincinnati is a decent fit. The Bengals rank 24th in EPA on short throws but 6th on deep throws, which matches a passer who lives under 10 yards. Their run defense ranks 28th by EPA and allows explosive runs at a high rate, which helps his scrambles and designed keepers. Their offense ranks 2nd in passing EPA and passes more than any team over expectation. Washington is a 6.5-point home underdog with a 52.5 total, so a trailing, pass-heavy script is plausible, the kind where his numbers have looked best.

The caution is the pass rush. Cincinnati sacks at the 9th-best rate, and Washington's line is without Tunsil (IR) and guard Lucas Patrick (out, concussion). Pass-rusher Cashius Howell is on IR for the Bengals, which helps a little. Washington is also without running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt, still on IR, and backup tight end Colson Yankoff. Cincinnati's secondary could get corner Jalen Davis back from IR, and safety Kyle Dugger, a part-timer, is out.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati gives up positive EPA on short throws while clamping down deep, which steers any QB toward exactly what Mariota does best. McLaurin underneath and tight ends should find room, since Cincinnati ranks 30th in what it lets the top tight end score over his average.

keyMatchups.title: Patched line vs a sacking defense
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati's sack rate ranks 9th, and Washington is protecting without Tunsil and Patrick. Mariota already faced the league's heaviest pressure rate in a small sample. This is where his outlier sack avoidance is most likely to break.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati's offense is 2nd in EPA and the league's strongest pass-over-expectation team, and the total sits at 52.5. If Washington trails, the backup's role, should he get one, becomes volume passing in catch-up mode.

nextGame.watch: Daniels' status on the late-week injury report: Mariota's relevance for Week 11 hinges entirely on it.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as Daniels is healthy, Mariota's rest of season is snap-free insurance, and the projections below describe what to expect only if he is pressed into starts. In that case, the sustainable parts are the short-area accuracy, a willingness to take what's there, and real rushing value. Together those make him a roughly average starter, as he was in 2025 at 188.3 passing yards a game.

What will regress: the zero interceptions, the 7.8% TD rate built on a handful of deep and red-zone throws, and above all the sack avoidance behind a line missing its left tackle. Expect something like 170-230 passing yards, about one touchdown a game with occasional picks, and 15-35 rushing yards as a starter.

confidence.note: Backup QB, 51 attempts across three mixed-role games; any outlook depends on Daniels' health.
